title: The Queen's Gambit Declined
standfirst: If you play 1…e5 against 1.e4 because it's the straightforward, classical answer, this is the equivalent against 1.d4.

steps.title: The other first move
body: 1.d4 leads to slower, more structural games than 1.e4. You need an answer, and this is the one that has never been refuted.
One thing to settle immediately: the Queen's Gambit is not really a gambit.

steps.title: The queen's pawn opening
body: Unlike 1.e4, this pawn is defended from the start — by the queen. That's why 1.d4 games tend to be slower.

steps.title: Mirror it
body: Black takes his share, defended by his own queen.

steps.title: The offer that isn't
body: White attacks d5 from the side, inviting …dxc4. But you cannot keep that pawn: after …dxc4 White plays e3 and Bxc4, regaining it with a strong centre.
So it's a gambit in name only — really it's a way to deflect Black's d-pawn and take over the centre.

steps.title: Refuse politely
body: Black declines, reinforcing d5 with a pawn. Solid and correct — though note it does shut in the c8 bishop, the same complaint as the French. The Slav study shows the alternative.

steps.title: A third attacker on d5
body: White keeps the pressure on the one contested square.

steps.title: A second defender
body: Black matches him, and develops toward the centre.

steps.title: Attack the defender
body: The same idea as the Ruy López's Bb5, one file over: don't attack the pawn, attack what defends it. The f6 knight is now pinned against the queen and can't easily move.
Pins on a defender are worth more than pins on nothing.

steps.title: Break the sting
body: Black doesn't try to escape the pin — he defuses it. With the bishop on e7 the knight is defended, so Bxf6 no longer wins anything and merely trades a good bishop for a knight.

steps.title: The modest move
body: It shuts in the c1 bishop, which is why beginners dislike it — but that bishop is already outside on g5. There's nothing left to shut in, so the move is simply solid.

steps.title: Tuck the king away
body: Black is fully developed on the kingside and completely safe. Nothing has gone wrong, which is the entire point of this opening.

steps.title: Finish the job
body: The last minor piece comes out. Both sides have played only sensible moves and both are fine.

steps.title: Ask the bishop the question
body: Black finally puts the question to the pinning bishop. White usually plays Bh4 to keep the pin, and the middlegame begins.
White's plan is the minority attack — pushing the b-pawn to create a weakness on c6. Black plays in the centre or on the kingside. Solid, strategic, and famously hard to lose with.
